title: Elastics: Where God and Science Smooch
summary: Josh and Chuck explore elastic, from early loincloths and breeches through the union suit, ACE bandages, and looms, to the history of rubber: its discovery in the Americas, Charles Goodyear's vulcanization, the rubber band, World War Two synthetic rubber, and DuPont's invention of Spandex. The episode also covers the chemistry of elastomers and glass transition temperature, why elastic degrades, a pirate-history article, a Shark Tank tangent, Pat Benatar and the spandex rocker trend, and a listener email about the D.B. Cooper tie evidence.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to elastic
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about being sick, then introduce the topic of elastic and define it as rubber woven with another fabric to make stretchy cloth.

segments.title: History of underwear and elastic waistbands
segments.summary: The hosts trace underwear from breechcloths and loincloths, through Middle Ages braies, to the union suit, which is named for being one piece. They also discuss the drop seat flap and the union suit's origin in reaction to corsets.

segments.title: ACE bandage and looms
segments.summary: The ACE bandage is explained as an acronym for all cotton elastic, introduced by 3M in 1918, and the hosts describe how looms weave elastic fabric from warp and weft threads.

segments.title: Elastic in everyday clothing
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh note elastic appears in necks of shirts, shoe tongues, and jeans waistbands, and they return to the history of rubber.

segments.title: Pirates and the explorers who found rubber
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a National Endowment for the Humanities article arguing that the popular image of pirates formed in a single decade, then describe European explorers finding rubber in the Americas and the native uses of the rubber tree's latex.

segments.title: Early rubber problems and the rubber name
segments.summary: Early raw rubber became brittle in cool temperatures outside the tropics. Joseph Priestley's pencil-erasing use is given as the origin of the word rubber.

segments.title: Charles Goodyear and vulcanization
segments.summary: Charles Goodyear spent years in poverty and debtor's prison working on rubber and found vulcanization by heating latex with sulfur. Thomas Hancock and Charles Macintosh had related work, and Hancock reverse engineered the process. Goodyear lost his patent case and died in debt, but his family later got royalties.

segments.title: Shark Tank tangent and Steve Miller aside
segments.summary: A tangent about entrepreneurs on Shark Tank giving up equity, and a brief aside about Steve Miller's Rock and Roll Hall of Fame remarks.

segments.title: Rubber industry, rubber trees in Southeast Asia, and World War Two
segments.summary: British smugglers took rubber seeds to Southeast Asia in the 1870s, shifting the rubber trade to Malaysia, Singapore and Sri Lanka. Automobiles increased demand, and Japan's invasion of the Pacific during World War Two cut off supply, prompting US companies to develop synthetic rubber.

segments.title: Rubber bands
segments.summary: Stephen Perry and Thomas Barnes invented the modern rubber band by slicing rings from vulcanized rubber tubing. The hosts describe how rubber bands are made today using a mandrel and heat.

segments.title: Synthetic rubber, Spandex, and elastomer chemistry
segments.summary: Synthetic rubbers developed in World War Two were not elastic enough for textiles until DuPont created Spandex in 1959. The hosts explain elastomers, their stretch and snap-back, glass transition temperature, and why rubber degrades from oxidation, ozone, UV light, and cold.

segments.title: Pat Benatar and the spandex rocker trend
segments.summary: Pat Benatar reportedly began the eighties spandex rocker trend after wearing a spandex costume at Catch a Rising Star on Halloween in 1978 and getting a strong response.

segments.title: Listener mail on Charlie Chaplin body robbers and D.B. Cooper tie
segments.summary: A listener notes that Charlie Chaplin's body robbery partner's name, Gancho Genev, means thief in Bulgarian. Another listener mention concerns new evidence on D.B. Cooper's tie linked to Boeing work, and a non-binary listener asks to be referred to with they/them pronouns.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh gives social media and contact information and signs off.
